newsitem.title: UK: OPTIONS - Bund option vols lower after FOMC.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - Bund option vols lower after FOMC.

text.p: Implied volatility of German Bund options eased on Wednesday as debt markets drew comfort from the the U.S. Federal Reserve's decision to keep interest rates on hold, options brokers said.
Brokers said options markets stirred to life with the short sterling market registering one of its busiest days of the year, after the Fed surprised many with its decision on Tuesday.
"Bund volatility will continue on a downward trend," said Luke White, broker at Fimat Futures UK.
He said local investors had started to sell Bund option volatility after remaining firm earlier in the day.

"But at certain levels it will rebound and continental banks will get involved in buying volatility and perhaps gamma trading, especially in the light of problems with Russia and the U.S. elections," White said.
Gamma measures is the rate of change between delta and an underlying market while delta measures the rate of change between options prices and the underlying market.
White said implied volatility of November options on December Bund futures was around 4.40 percent compared with 4.66 percent at Tuesday's close.
On the slightly less popular December options, implied volatility was down to 4.62 percent from Tuesday's 4.97 percent, he added.

Analysts said investors were back hedging their overall bond positions with markets likely to remain nervous over inflation and monetary policy until the next Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting on November 13.
Mark Robinson, options broker at HSBC Futures, said volatilities had come down only slightly since Tuesday, mainly because they had not really spiked up before the FOMC meeting.
"If they had moved up more you would have seen more unwinding, but given they only ticked up then there was no reason to see them come down more," Robinson said.
Robinson said volatility might drift slightly lower in the next week or two.

But if more strong U.S. economic data appeared, starting with September U.S. non-farm payrolls due on October 4, sentiment concerning the need for an interest rate rise would start to build again before the FOMC November meeting.
"If they had raised rates on Tuesday, the act would have been done and you might have had more volatility over the next day or so while the market readjusted," Robinson said.
"But this (the FOMC stance) leaves it all open and the next (rate) move is still up," he said.
Robinson said such a situation "will always keep volatility ready to squeeze higher" against the general bond market trend toward lower volatility in the past few months.
White said short sterling futures had one of the busiest days of the year due to bearish trades. Buying of 94.00 and even 93.75 December put spreads were popular.
He added the British government's internal political problems over European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) made gilts an exception to mainland European moves to lower volatility.
Implied volatility on December 107-00 gilts was 6.5 percent, unchanged from Tuesday's close.
In Bund options he said U.S. houses had bought about 2,000 lots of November Bund 99.00 calls, but there was no trade in puts at that strike price.
--Stephen Nisbet International Bonds Unit +44 171 542 6320
